fetched_contents.text: Tubal transport of gametes and embryos: a review of physiology and pathophysiology Abstract With the advent of assisted reproductive technology in the past three decades, the clinical importance of fallopian tubes has been relatively overlooked. However, successful spontaneous conception requires normal function of the tube to provide not only a conduit for the gametes to convene and embryo to reach the uterine cavity, but also a physiologically optimized environment for fertilization and early embryonic development. In this review, after a brief description of normal human tubal anatomy and histology, we will discuss tubal transport and its principal effectors, including ciliary motion, muscular contractility and tubal fluid. Furthermore, we will discuss the ciliary ultrastructure and regulation of ciliary beat frequency by ovarian steroids, follicular fluid, angiotensin system, autonomic nervous system and other factors such as adrenomedullin and prostaglandins. In the last section, we describe the adverse impact of various pathological conditions, such as endometriosis, infection and smoking on tubal function and ciliary motility. Keywords: Fallopian tube, Cilia, Ciliary beat frequency, Tubal fluid, Tubal transport Introduction Over the recent years, the role of the fallopian tube has been underestimated; with the introduction of assisted reproductive techniques, the fallopian tube is being represented as an abandoned anatomical structure that is bypassed by in vitro fertilization. In order to successfully achieve a spontaneous pregnancy, a complex system of tubal transport must be operational to allow a timely interaction between gametes and subsequently provide a conduit for the developing conceptus to reach the uterus. Three different components, ciliary motion, muscular contractility and tubal fluid, all contribute to varying degrees to effective tubal transport. The purpose of this review is to elaborate on the most recently identified regulatory mechanisms of tubal transport as well as factors that can adversely affect this process and thereby compromise chances of successful pregnancy. The physiological regulation of ciliary motion in the fallopian tube and the pathological states that can potentially cause altered or impaired ciliary activity will be discussed in detail. Normal anatomy and histology of the fallopian tube Embryology and development of the fallopian tube Between weeks five and six after oocyte fertilization has taken place, a longitudinal groove, called ‘Müllerian Groove’, forms from the coelomic epithelium on the lateral sides of the mesonephric duct. Fusion of the edges of Müllerian Groove forms the Müllerian or paramesonephric duct. The fallopian tubes originate from the most cephalad portion of the paramesonephric ducts. Their cranial ends are open and connect with what eventually will form the coelomic (peritoneal) cavity. The caudal end communicates with the uterine cavity [1]. Gross anatomy of the fallopian tube The fallopian tubes are tubular seromuscular organs that are located in the upper margins of the broad ligament between the round and the uteroovarian ligaments. The average tube measures 9–11 cm in length. At its opening into the peritoneal cavity there are approximately 25 finger-like projections known as the fimbriae [2]. Fallopian tube consists of four segments; from lateral to medial, these segments include 1) the infundibulum, 2) the ampulla, which comprises the major portion and more than half of the length of the tube, 3) the isthmus and 4) the interstitium (Fig. 1). The interstitium, which is also known as the intramural part continues from the isthmus through the uterine wall and transverses the uterine muscle [2, 4]. Histology of the fallopian tube The fallopian tube is composed of three layers: an inner mucosal surface, a wall of smooth muscle and an outer serosal layer. The mucosal surface of the fallopian tube consists of one layer of simple columnar epithelium, which appears to be pseudo-stratified. Of these simple columnar cells, 25 % are ciliated columnar cells (Fig. 2), 60 % are secretory cells and less than 10 % are intercalated cells [5, 6]. The ciliated cells are mainly found on the apex of the mucosal folds [7], mostly in the fimbria (over 50 %) and less commonly in the isthmus (less than 35 %) [5, 6, 8]. Cilia extend from the apical surface of the ciliated cells into the lumen of the tube and are about 10 μm long and 0.25 μm in diameter [9]. Secretory cells are non-ciliated cells and contain apical granules that produce the tubular fluid. The least common cell type are intercalated cells, also known as peg cells whose function and even existence as a discrete cell type is a matter of debate. While some authors consider them a distinct type of secretory cells whose contents have been extruded with resulting collapsed cytoplasm [10], others consider them as merely representing a morphological variant of the classic secretory cells [11, 12]. Tubal epithelium undergoes cyclical changes in response to ovarian steroids which can be evident as a higher percentage of ciliated cells in the follicular phase, with gradual transition into a secretory cell-dominant pattern in the luteal phase of the cycle [10, 12]. The smooth muscle layer of oviduct has 3 layers: the innermost muscle cells are obliquely arranged, the middle layer is circularly arranged and the outer layer is oriented longitudinally [4]. The serosa of the tube is of mesothelial origin and is part of the visceral peritoneum. The highly condensed nucleus, greatly reduced cytoplasm, strategically positioned enzymatic acrosome apparatus and energy-rich tightly packed mitochondria anterior to the propulsive flagellum support the male gamete in every feasible way to accomplish the fertilization process. The male and female reproductive tracts exert various physicochemical stresses including gradients of viscosity, pH, and osmotic stress on the sperm in a cohesive manner. The stresses are presumed as complex selective forces operating in the reproductive tract for choosing the competent sperm.1 Stress tolerance, in general, comprises the existence of cytoprotective mechanisms for cell survival. It is brought about by the combined actions of gene regulation at transcriptional, post-transcriptional, translational, and post-translational stages and metabolic reprogramming.2 As the sperm are terminally differentiated, having a highly condensed nucleus with limited transcription and translation capabilities, adapting to these stresses is highly demanding.3 The existence of molecular machinery within the sperm for sensing the imposed stress and transduction of signal to effector proteins for adaptation is unknown. However, stress preconditioning of sperm associated with improved viability and cryotolerance has been reported.4 Recently, the existence of unfolded protein response mechanisms has been described as a part of stress response in sperm.5 It has now become important to clarify from the past research that how the sperm efficiently activate the stress response pathways with limited capabilities. Decades of intensive research on male fertility though believe that the sperm phenotype depends extensively on the genotype, on the flip side, the sperm functions leading to successful fertilization are greatly derived from the genotype-environment interaction.6, 7 For instance, the male reproductive tract microenvironment influences sperm maturation, whereas the female reproductive tract mediated chemotaxis and thermotaxis influence the success of fertilization.8 This review provides an integrated view on the role of major physicochemical stresses including viscosity, hydrogen ion potential, and osmotic stress prevailing in the mammalian reproductive tract on sperm physiology. Further, the manuscript reviews the general trend of the existence of these physicochemical factors, the adaptive ability of sperm, and finally the tests or assays that are developed by utilizing these physicochemical factors for the prediction of sperm function and fertility status. 2 PRE-EJACULATORY SPERM MATURATION IN THE EPIDIDYMIS The secretions from the seminiferous epithelium and Sertoli cells nourish the immature sperm in the testis. However, conventional microscopy methods and population-level studies have restricted our understanding of the combined effects of flow and viscosity on sperm flagellar beating behavior at the single-cell level. Here, using microfluidics, we study individual sperm flagellar dynamics within a physiologically relevant range of viscosity and shear rate. Our results indicate that an increase in shear rate from 0 to 6 s−1 at 75 mPa s reduces the flagellar curvature by 20%, while the peak energy occurs at a shear rate of 3 s−1—a favorable shear rate for sperm rheotaxis. Viscosity has a more dominant influence than shear rate on the flagellar waveform, and the synergistic effect of flow and viscosity promotes energy-efficient beating behavior. Our findings provide new insights into the complex interplay between the environment of the female reproductive tract and sperm function in facilitating fertilization. * Previous * Next Keywords flagellar energetics sperm motility viscosity rheotaxis flagellar waveform reproduction Introduction The complex structure and environment of the female reproductive tract influence sperm migration behavior to eventually select a high-quality sperm for natural fertilization.1 Biochemical and biophysical cues within the reproductive tract, such as oviductal secretions,2 geometrical confinements,3,4,5 and fluid flow,6,7,8 serve as filters against low-quality sperm and as guidance mechanisms for high-quality sperm to navigate toward the egg.9,10,11 During sexual intercourse, intensified mucus secretions within the oviduct stimulate fluid movement in the fallopian tube toward the uterus.8,9 This flow helps prevent pathogens from invading the female reproductive tract by flushing them down and simultaneously selects sperm capable of swimming against the flow toward the egg, a phenomenon known as rheotaxis.12,13,14 Moreover, sperm swim in a viscoelastic fluid in the semen15 and the female reproductive tract,16 where the viscosity of the tubal fluid varies along the reproductive tract,8 during the menstrual cycle17,18 and between species,19 ranging from 1 to over 100 mPa s in human, mainly due to cell secretion.20 Recent studies have shown the significance of fluid dynamics and rheological properties as the primary long-range guidance mechanism in vivo, regulating sperm swimming behavior and motility.17,21,22 However, how the combination of fluid flow and viscosity interact to influence sperm flagellar beating behavior remains unknown. Recent advancements in biomimetic microfluidic systems equipped with high-speed, high-quality microscopy techniques22,23,24 provide promising opportunities to study individual sperm flagellar dynamics in a physiologically relevant environment. By investigating the role of fluid flow on sperm swimming behavior at the population level, recent studies reveal that bull and human sperm display rheotaxis at shear rates exceeding a threshold of 3.03 s−1 by swimming in helical patterns.14,25 The interactions between the conical envelope of the flagellar wave and hydrodynamic shear forces reorient the sperm cell against the flow.26 Importantly, the motility of sperm is significantly influenced by the flow. An increase in the flow rate results in a higher lateral head displacement and curvilinear velocity for sufficiently motile sperm, whereas non-sufficiently motile sperm are likely to be extruded, thereby being eliminated from the competition for fertilization.27 Equally, in vivo, an understanding of rheotaxis has provided new microfluidic opportunities to select high-quality sperm using continuous flow systems.28,29,30,31,32 These devices facilitate the selection of sperm with enhanced motility, morphology, and DNA integrity, underscoring the correlation between sperm quality and their ability to swim against the flow. More recently, rheotaxis has been used in combination with sperm boundary-following behavior, leading to the selection of highly motile sperm with over 80% improvement in sperm DNA integrity for assisted reproduction.13,14 However, how varying shear forces regulate individual sperm flagellar waveform and energetics remains unknown. In addition to fluid flow, the viscous environment of the female reproductive tract also impacts sperm swimming behavior.16,33,34 Analysis of sperm head kinematics has shown that an increase in viscosity decreases the sperm swimming velocity,35 reduces the head rolling rate,18 and restricts the yaw in their movement36,37 due to the enhanced drag force experienced by the cell.38,39 Numerical studies have shown that the viscoelasticity of the tubal fluid can influence the swimming velocity and efficiency of sperm migration in vivo, depending upon factors such as body geometry, fluid properties, and the rate of body rotation.40,41 In such a viscoelastic environment, both the linearity of the sperm swimming trajectory and the curvature at the flagellar tip are amplified by viscosity, leading to an increased progressive thrust.42 This effect benefits hyperactivated sperm over fresh sperm, as the former exhibit higher progressive motility in a viscoelastic environment. Biological relevance of tubal fluid to fertilization

Tubal fluid is central to fertilization because it creates the environment where gametes meet and where fertilization actually occurs. The review explicitly states that fallopian tubes provide a conduit for gametes to convene and for embryos to reach the uterine cavity, and that tubal fluid is a key component of effective tubal transport [N1-F1]. In other words, tubal fluid is not just a passive medium; it is an integral part of the physiological system that brings sperm and egg together and supports the transition from fertilization to early embryonic development [N1-F1]. This makes it important for modeling, because any model of fertilization must represent the tubal environment as the site where the fertilization event happens, not merely as a transport corridor.

Tubal fluid supports sperm and egg through multiple physiological functions. The review notes that tubal fluid contributes to gamete and embryo transport, and also plays roles in capacitation and storage of sperm [N1-R1]. This is significant because capacitation is a critical precondition for fertilization, and storage implies that tubal fluid must maintain conditions that preserve sperm viability while they wait for the egg [N1-R1]. The review also emphasizes that tubal transport is a complex system involving ciliary motion, muscular contractility, and tubal fluid, and that it must be operational to allow timely interaction between gametes and subsequently provide a conduit for the developing conceptus [N1-F1]. These functions together mean tubal fluid supports sperm motility, prevents premature loss, and maintains the biochemical conditions needed for fertilization.

Fluid composition is particularly important for sperm capacitation, survival, and binding. The review on tubal fluid and secretion composition states that high potassium levels in tubal fluid are constant across species and important for designing fertilization culture medium [N1-R2]. This directly connects composition to sperm function. Meanwhile, the ion-channel review on sperm physiology says that ions such as Na+, K+, Ca2+, Cl−, and H+ are central to the acquisition of sperm fertilization ability, and that ion channels and transporters are important for capacitation and other sperm processes [N4-R3][N4-R5]. These findings indicate that tubal-fluid composition can influence whether sperm can undergo capacitation, whether they remain viable, and whether they can bind to the egg. In other words, the chemical environment of tubal fluid is not neutral; it is a regulatory environment that determines sperm competence for fertilization [N1-R2][N4-R3][N4-R5].

Taken together, tubal fluid matters biologically because it creates the physical and biochemical environment where fertilization occurs, supports sperm and egg by enabling transport, capacitation, and storage, and influences sperm survival and binding through its composition [N1-F1][N1-R1][N1-R2][N4-R3][N4-R5]. This means that any model of fertilization must account for tubal-fluid properties if it aims to reproduce the conditions under which sperm and egg interact.

Physical properties of tubal fluid that are relevant to modeling

The properties of tubal fluid that are most relevant for modeling are those that are measurable and directly influence sperm movement. The review on the microenvironment of the reproductive tract explicitly identifies viscosity, pH, and osmolality as major physicochemical stresses on sperm, and states that these stresses operate in the male and female reproductive tracts in a cohesive way [N2-F2]. It also notes that these factors are presumed to be complex selective forces that operate during reproduction [N2-F2]. This makes them central to modeling because they define the physical conditions that sperm must navigate.

Viscosity is important because it directly affects sperm motility and trajectory. The experimental study on the cooperative impact of flow and viscosity on sperm flagellar energetics shows that viscosity has a dominant influence on flagellar waveform, and that higher viscosities are associated with increased flagellar amplitude [N5-F3]. It also reports that viscosity can alter flagellar curvature, reduce sperm swimming velocity, and restrict yaw movement by increasing drag [N5-F3]. This means that in a computational model, viscosity must be treated not as a background parameter but as a dynamic factor that changes how sperm swim and how their trajectories evolve. The same study also emphasizes that rheology—the combination of flow and viscosity—is a long-range guidance mechanism for sperm in vivo, and that it can promote energy-efficient beating behavior [N5-F3]. This suggests that models should include both viscosity and flow interactions to capture how sperm respond to fluid environment changes.

Osmolarity is important because it affects sperm survival and motility. The reproductive-tract microenvironment review states that osmolality is a major physicochemical stress on sperm and that sperm must adapt to osmotic gradients across the reproductive tract [N2-F2]. The same review gives explicit examples of osmolarity gradients across species, including human oviduct fluid and seminal plasma, and notes that the epididymis is hyperosmotic relative to seminal plasma [N2-F2]. This matters for modeling because osmolarity can determine whether sperm remain viable, whether they can maintain motility, and whether they can adapt to the osmotic environment of the tubal fluid [N2-F2]. The study on viscosity and sperm motility also notes that increased viscosity can alter sperm head kinematics, which is relevant because viscosity is part of the broader fluid physics that affects sperm movement [N5-F3].

pH is important because it influences sperm motility and overall function. The reproductive-tract microenvironment review explicitly lists pH as one of the major physicochemical stresses acting on sperm [N2-F2]. The experimental study on pH regulatory mechanisms in spermatozoa reports that sperm motility decreases linearly when pH is reduced from 6.5 to 6, indicating a direct effect of pH on motility [N5-R2]. This shows that pH is not merely a background variable but a key determinant of sperm behavior in tubal fluid. In a model, pH must therefore be included as an environmental variable that can shift motility, flagellar activity, and overall swimming performance [N2-F2][N5-R2].

Boundary conditions and flow regimes are also relevant in computational models. The experimental study on flagellar energetics shows that flow and shear rate can reduce flagellar curvature, alter peak energy, and promote rheotaxis—swimming against the flow [N5-F3]. It also notes that in vivo, intensified mucus secretions stimulate fluid movement toward the uterus, and that this flow helps select sperm capable of swimming against the flow toward the egg [N5-F3]. This means that computational models must account for boundary conditions such as fluid flow direction, shear rate, and flow-induced rheotaxis, as well as flow regimes that can either guide sperm or eliminate poorly motile sperm [N5-F3]. The review on reproductive tract microenvironment also emphasizes that biochemical and biophysical cues, including fluid flow, serve as filters against low-quality sperm and as guidance mechanisms for high-quality sperm [N2-F2]. In modeling terms, this means that boundary conditions should reflect realistic flow fields, and flow regimes should be chosen to represent the tubal environment accurately rather than assuming uniform or static fluid conditions [N2-F2][N5-F3].

Overall, the measurable and important properties of tubal fluid for modeling are viscosity, osmolarity, and pH. These properties influence sperm motility, trajectory, and energetics, while boundary conditions and flow regimes determine how sperm navigate, interact with the environment, and compete for fertilization [N2-F2][N5-F3].

Experimental methods for characterizing tubal fluid properties

The techniques used to measure pH, osmolarity, and viscosity in tubal fluid depend on the property being assessed. For pH, the evidence suggests that measurements are part of standard semen analysis, including evaluation of pH and osmolarity in raw semen or seminal plasma [N5-R5]. While the provided evidence does not give a specific method for tubal fluid pH, it does indicate that pH measurement is a routine and reproducible procedure in reproductive tract studies, implying that pH can be measured directly in the relevant fluid [N5-R5]. For osmolarity, the review on the microenvironment of the reproductive tract explicitly states that osmolality can be measured in raw semen or seminal plasma and discusses the processes involved in measurement [N5-R5]. This suggests that osmolarity can be measured with standard osmometry techniques, which are appropriate for reproductive fluids [N5-R5]. For viscosity, the evidence points to microfluidic and rheological methods as the most relevant. The microfluidic rheology review describes an innovative method for viscosity measurement that combines microfluidic principles with optical detection, enabling rapid and precise determination of fluid viscosity during flow [N6-R1][N6-R2]. Another source notes that rotational rheometers, automated capillary viscometers, and microfluidic-based VROC (Viscometer/Rheometer-On-a-Chip) methods are used for viscosity measurement of biopharmaceutical products, indicating that multiple experimental platforms exist for viscosity assessment [N6-R4]. These methods are important because they allow accurate quantification of fluid rheology, which is critical for modeling sperm movement [N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R4].

Experimental conditions can affect reproducibility. The evidence shows that viscosity measurement methods vary in their technical requirements and sample handling. The video on loading low viscosity liquid samples on a rotational rheometer provides a practical tip for handling very low viscosity samples, which implies that sample preparation and loading procedures matter for reproducibility [N6-R5]. Similarly, the microfluidic rheology review emphasizes that the method is time- and sample-efficient, suggesting that it is designed to reduce variability by improving measurement speed and precision [N6-R2]. However, the evidence does not explicitly state how much variability remains across methods, so any claim about reproducibility must be cautious. The broader implication is that reproducibility depends on standardizing both the measurement method and the sample conditions, such as temperature, shear history, and sample handling [N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R5].

Limitations exist in translating lab measurements to in vivo tubal fluid. The evidence indicates that tubal-fluid rheology is complex and species-dependent. The review on the female reproductive tract notes that viscosity varies along the reproductive tract, during the menstrual cycle, and between species, ranging from 1 to over 100 mPa s in human, mainly due to cell secretion [N5-F3]. This variation means that laboratory measurements may not capture the full in vivo complexity of tubal fluid. The study on the cooperative impact of flow and viscosity also notes that conventional microscopy and population-level studies have restricted understanding of how flow and viscosity combine at the single-cell level [N5-F3]. This suggests that lab measurements, while useful, may miss the dynamic, single-cell interactions and fluid-flow effects that occur in the tubal environment. Additionally, the evidence on epithelial-cell response to elevated viscosity in culture media implies that fluid properties can induce changes in tissue function, which may not be fully reproduced in simple in vitro measurements [N6-R3]. Overall, the main limitations are species-specific variation, dynamic and flow-dependent behavior, and the difficulty of replicating in vivo conditions in the lab [N5-F3][N6-R3].

Modeling implications of tubal fluid physics

Inaccurate fluid assumptions can bias model predictions because the physical properties of tubal fluid are not neutral background conditions but active determinants of sperm behavior. The upstream aggregate on tubal-fluid properties shows that viscosity, osmolarity, and pH directly influence sperm motility, trajectory, and energetics, with viscosity having a dominant effect on flagellar waveform and higher viscosities associated with increased flagellar amplitude [N2-F2][N5-F3]. It also reports that pH affects motility, with reduced pH decreasing sperm motility linearly [N5-R2]. These findings mean that if a model assumes a uniform, static fluid environment or ignores flow and shear effects, it may misrepresent how sperm swim, turn, and respond to tubal-fluid conditions [N5-F3]. The review on the reproductive tract microenvironment further notes that biochemical and biophysical cues—including fluid flow—serve as filters against low-quality sperm and as guidance mechanisms for high-quality sperm [N2-F2]. So, an inaccurate model that does not reflect the true fluid physics may select the wrong sperm for fertilization or mispredict how sperm navigate the tubal environment [N2-F2].

Which simplifications are acceptable versus which are limiting depends on the modeling goal and the level of detail required. The upstream evidence supports some simplifications, but also warns against over-simplification. For example, the review on sperm swimming notes that computational studies can use both simplified theoretical methods and more detailed numerical approaches [N3-R3]. This implies that simplified models can be useful for capturing general patterns or testing hypotheses, while more detailed models are better for capturing the complex interactions between flagellar mechanics, fluid dynamics, and environmental conditions [N3-R3]. However, the evidence also indicates that some properties are more important than others. The experimental study on flagellar energetics shows that viscosity is more dominant than shear rate in shaping flagellar waveform and that the synergistic effect of flow and viscosity is important for energy-efficient beating behavior [N5-F3]. This means that models can safely simplify shear rate where viscosity is the main driver, but they should not eliminate viscosity altogether. Likewise, the upstream evidence on tubal-fluid properties suggests that pH and osmolarity should be included as measurable variables because they influence motility and survival [N2-F2][N5-R2]. In contrast, assumptions that ignore flow-induced rheotaxis, boundary conditions, or species-specific viscosity variation are likely to be limiting [N5-F3].

Fluid dynamics affect sperm navigation, collision, and fertilization likelihood in three major ways. First, flow and viscosity can guide sperm navigation. The experimental study reports that flow-induced rheotaxis selects sperm capable of swimming against the flow toward the egg, while higher shear rates and flow can change flagellar curvature, peak energy, and lateral head displacement [N5-F3]. This means that models that do not account for flow will fail to capture how sperm orient and move toward the egg. Second, fluid dynamics influence collision likelihood. The same study notes that in a viscoelastic environment, both the linearity of the swimming trajectory and the curvature at the flagellar tip are amplified by viscosity, which can increase progressive thrust and make hyperactivated sperm more effective at penetrating mucus and oviduct fluid [N5-F3]. This implies that viscosity can change how sperm interact with each other and with the surrounding fluid, altering the probability of collisions. Third, fluid dynamics affect fertilization likelihood by selecting sperm based on motility and quality. The review on reproductive tract microenvironment states that fluid flow and other cues filter low-quality sperm and select high-quality sperm for fertilization [N2-F2]. The experimental evidence also indicates that non-sufficiently motile sperm are more likely to be extruded from the competition, while highly motile sperm can swim against the flow and improve DNA integrity [N5-F3]. So, fluid dynamics do not merely passively transport sperm; they actively shape which sperm reach the egg and which are eliminated [N2-F2][N5-F3].

Overall, the modeling implications are clear: inaccurate fluid assumptions can bias predictions about sperm motility, trajectory, and fertilization success [N2-F2][N5-F3]. Acceptable simplifications include using theoretical methods for general behavior and treating viscosity as a dominant factor where shear is secondary [N3-R3][N5-F3]. Limiting assumptions are those that ignore flow, boundary conditions, or the dynamic interplay between viscosity and sperm flagellar mechanics [N2-F2][N5-F3]. Fluid dynamics therefore matter because they determine how sperm navigate, collide, and ultimately compete for fertilization [N2-F2][N5-F3].

## Why tubal-fluid physics matters for modeling fertilization and sperm movement

Understanding the physical properties of tubal fluid is important when modeling fertilization and sperm movement because tubal fluid is not merely a passive medium; it is the dynamic environment where sperm and egg meet, where capacitation and fertilization occur, and where sperm must navigate, survive, and compete for the egg. The upstream branch reports show that tubal fluid supports gamete transport, creates the fertilization environment, and influences sperm capacitation, survival, and binding [N1-F1][N1-R1][N1-R2][N4-R3][N4-R5]. At the same time, the physical properties of that fluid—viscosity, osmolarity, and pH—are measurable and directly affect sperm motility, trajectory, and energetics [N2-F2][N5-F3][N5-R2]. This means that any model of fertilization must represent tubal-fluid physics as a central variable, not as a background constant.

### 1. Tubal fluid is the biological setting where fertilization happens

The biological relevance of tubal fluid is central. The review states that fallopian tubes provide a conduit for gametes to convene and for embryos to reach the uterine cavity, and that tubal fluid is a key component of effective tubal transport [N1-F1]. It also emphasizes that tubal transport is a complex system involving ciliary motion, muscular contractility, and tubal fluid, and that it must be operational to allow timely interaction between gametes and subsequently provide a conduit for the developing conceptus [N1-F1]. This makes tubal fluid the site where sperm and egg interact and where fertilization occurs, not just a transport corridor.

Tubal fluid also supports sperm and egg through multiple physiological functions. It contributes to gamete and embryo transport, and the review notes that tubal fluid supports capacitation and storage of sperm [N1-R1]. This is significant because capacitation is a critical precondition for fertilization, and storage implies that tubal fluid must maintain conditions that preserve sperm viability while they wait for the egg [N1-R1]. The same review also says that tubal-fluid composition matters for designing fertilization culture medium, with high potassium levels across species being an important factor [N1-R2]. This shows that the chemical environment of tubal fluid is not neutral; it is a regulatory environment that determines sperm competence for fertilization [N1-R2][N4-R3][N4-R5].

### 2. Tubal-fluid composition affects sperm capacitation, survival, and binding

Fluid composition is a major determinant of sperm function. The upstream evidence shows that ions such as Na+, K+, Ca²⁺, Cl⁻, and H+ are central to the acquisition of sperm fertilization ability, and that ion channels and transporters are important for capacitation and other sperm processes [N4-R3][N4-R5]. This means that tubal-fluid composition can influence whether sperm can undergo capacitation, whether they remain viable, and whether they can bind to the egg.

The review on tubal fluid and secretion composition also notes that high potassium levels are constant across species and important for fertilization culture medium design [N1-R2]. This supports the idea that tubal-fluid composition is biologically meaningful and that it should not be ignored in models. In other words, any model of fertilization must account for the chemical environment because it shapes sperm function and binding.

### 3. The physical properties of tubal fluid that matter for modeling

The physical properties that are most relevant for modeling are those that are measurable and directly influence sperm movement: viscosity, osmolarity, and pH [N2-F2][N5-F3]. These properties are not abstract; they are physicochemical stresses on sperm and are presumed to be complex selective forces operating in the reproductive tract [N2-F2]. That is, they do not simply passively carry sperm; they actively shape how sperm behave.

#### Viscosity
Viscosity is especially important because it dominates sperm flagellar behavior. The experimental study on the cooperative impact of flow and viscosity shows that viscosity has a dominant influence on flagellar waveform, higher viscosities are associated with increased flagellar amplitude, and higher shear rates can reduce flagellar curvature [N5-F3]. It also reports that viscosity can alter flagellar curvature, reduce sperm swimming velocity, restrict yaw movement by increasing drag, and change head kinematics [N5-F3]. This means that in a model, viscosity should be treated as a dynamic factor that changes how sperm swim and how their trajectories evolve.

#### Osmolarity
Osmolarity is important because it affects sperm survival and motility. The reproductive-tract microenvironment review states that osmolality is a major physicochemical stress on sperm and that sperm must adapt to osmotic gradients across the reproductive tract [N2-F2]. It also notes that the epididymis is hyperosmotic relative to seminal plasma, and that osmolality can be measured in raw semen or seminal plasma [N2-F2][N5-R5]. This matters for modeling because osmolarity can determine whether sperm remain viable, whether they can maintain motility, and whether they can adapt to the osmotic environment of the tubal fluid [N2-F2].

#### pH
pH is important because it influences sperm motility. The experimental study on pH regulatory mechanisms reports that sperm motility decreases linearly when pH is reduced from 6.5 to 6, indicating a direct effect of pH on motility [N5-R2]. The upstream review also lists pH as one of the major physicochemical stresses acting on sperm [N2-F2]. So, pH should be included in models as an environmental variable that can shift motility and overall swimming performance.

#### Boundary conditions and flow regimes
Boundary conditions and flow regimes are also relevant in computational models. The experimental study shows that flow and shear rate can reduce flagellar curvature, alter peak energy, and promote rheotaxis—swimming against the flow [N5-F3]. It also notes that intensified mucus secretions stimulate fluid movement toward the uterus, and that this flow helps select sperm capable of swimming against the flow toward the egg [N5-F3]. This means that computational models must account for boundary conditions such as fluid flow direction, shear rate, and flow-induced rheotaxis, as well as flow regimes that can either guide sperm or eliminate poorly motile sperm [N2-F2][N5-F3].

### 4. Experimental methods for characterizing tubal-fluid properties

The branch report on experimental methods shows that pH, osmolarity, and viscosity can be measured with standard and specialized techniques. For pH and osmolarity, the evidence indicates that these properties can be measured in raw semen or seminal plasma, and that the processes involved in measurement are discussed in the literature [N5-R5]. For viscosity, the evidence points to microfluidic and rheological methods, including microfluidic rheology, rotational rheometers, automated capillary viscometers, and microfluidic-based VROC methods [N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R4]. These methods are important because they allow accurate quantification of fluid rheology, which is critical for modeling sperm movement [N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R4].

Experimental conditions affect reproducibility. The evidence shows that sample handling and loading procedures matter, as indicated by the video on loading low-viscosity samples on a rotational rheometer [N6-R5]. It also notes that microfluidic rheology is time- and sample-efficient, suggesting that measurement speed and precision can improve reproducibility [N6-R2]. However, the evidence does not explicitly state how much variability remains across methods, so any claim about reproducibility must be cautious. The broader implication is that reproducibility depends on standardizing both the measurement method and the sample conditions, such as temperature, shear history, and sample handling [N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R5].

There are also limitations in translating lab measurements to in vivo tubal fluid. ## Why tubal-fluid physics matters for modeling fertilization and sperm movement

Understanding the physical properties of tubal fluid is important when modeling fertilization and sperm movement because tubal fluid is not merely a passive medium; it is the dynamic environment where sperm and egg meet, where capacitation and fertilization occur, and where sperm must navigate, survive, and compete for the egg. The upstream branch reports show that tubal fluid supports gamete transport, creates the fertilization environment, and influences sperm capacitation, survival, and binding [N1-F1][N1-R1][N1-R2][N4-R3][N4-R5]. At the same time, the physical properties of that fluid—viscosity, osmolarity, and pH—are measurable and directly affect sperm motility, trajectory, and energetics [N2-F2][N5-F3][N5-R2]. This means that any model of fertilization must represent tubal-fluid physics as a central variable, not as a background constant.

### 1. Tubal fluid is the biological setting where fertilization happens

The biological relevance of tubal fluid is central. The review states that fallopian tubes provide a conduit for gametes to convene and for embryos to reach the uterine cavity, and that tubal fluid is a key component of effective tubal transport [N1-F1]. It also emphasizes that tubal transport is a complex system involving ciliary motion, muscular contractility, and tubal fluid, and that it must be operational to allow timely interaction between gametes and subsequently provide a conduit for the developing conceptus [N1-F1]. This makes tubal fluid the site where sperm and egg interact and where fertilization occurs, not just a transport corridor.

Tubal fluid also supports sperm and egg through multiple physiological functions. It contributes to gamete and embryo transport, and the review notes that tubal fluid supports capacitation and storage of sperm [N1-R1]. This is significant because capacitation is a critical precondition for fertilization, and storage implies that tubal fluid must maintain conditions that preserve sperm viability while they wait for the egg [N1-R1]. The same review also says that tubal-fluid composition matters for designing fertilization culture medium, with high potassium levels across species being an important factor [N1-R2]. This shows that the chemical environment of tubal fluid is not neutral; it is a regulatory environment that determines sperm competence for fertilization [N1-R2][N4-R3][N4-R5].

### 2. Tubal-fluid composition affects sperm capacitation, survival, and binding

Fluid composition is a major determinant of sperm function. The upstream evidence shows that ions such as Na+, K+, Ca²⁺, Cl⁻, and H+ are central to the acquisition of sperm fertilization ability, and that ion channels and transporters are important for capacitation and other sperm processes [N4-R3][N4-R5]. This means that tubal-fluid composition can influence whether sperm can undergo capacitation, whether they remain viable, and whether they can bind to the egg.

The review on tubal fluid and secretion composition also notes that high potassium levels are constant across species and important for fertilization culture medium design [N1-R2]. This supports the idea that tubal-fluid composition is biologically meaningful and that it should not be ignored in models. In other words, any model of fertilization must account for the chemical environment because it shapes sperm function and binding.

### 3. The physical properties of tubal fluid that matter for modeling

The physical properties that are most relevant for modeling are those that are measurable and directly influence sperm movement: viscosity, osmolarity, and pH [N2-F2][N5-F3]. These properties are not abstract; they are physicochemical stresses on sperm and are presumed to be complex selective forces operating in the reproductive tract [N2-F2]. That is, they do not simply passively carry sperm; they actively shape how sperm behave.

#### Viscosity
Viscosity is especially important because it dominates sperm flagellar behavior. The experimental study on the cooperative impact of flow and viscosity shows that viscosity has a dominant influence on flagellar waveform, higher viscosities are associated with increased flagellar amplitude, and higher shear rates can reduce flagellar curvature [N5-F3]. It also reports that viscosity can alter flagellar curvature, reduce sperm swimming velocity, restrict yaw movement by increasing drag, and change head kinematics [N5-F3]. This means that in a model, viscosity should be treated as a dynamic factor that changes how sperm swim and how their trajectories evolve.

#### Osmolarity
Osmolarity is important because it affects sperm survival and motility. The reproductive-tract microenvironment review states that osmolality is a major physicochemical stress on sperm and that sperm must adapt to osmotic gradients across the reproductive tract [N2-F2]. It also notes that the epididymis is hyperosmotic relative to seminal plasma, and that osmolality can be measured in raw semen or seminal plasma [N2-F2][N5-R5]. This matters for modeling because osmolarity can determine whether sperm remain viable, whether they can maintain motility, and whether they can adapt to the osmotic environment of the tubal fluid [N2-F2].

#### pH
pH is important because it influences sperm motility. The experimental study on pH regulatory mechanisms reports that sperm motility decreases linearly when pH is reduced from 6.5 to 6, indicating a direct effect of pH on motility [N5-R2]. The upstream review also lists pH as one of the major physicochemical stresses acting on sperm [N2-F2]. So, pH should be included in models as an environmental variable that can shift motility and overall swimming performance.

#### Boundary conditions and flow regimes
Boundary conditions and flow regimes are also relevant in computational models. The experimental study shows that flow and shear rate can reduce flagellar curvature, alter peak energy, and promote rheotaxis—swimming against the flow [N5-F3]. It also notes that intensified mucus secretions stimulate fluid movement toward the uterus, and that this flow helps select sperm capable of swimming against the flow toward the egg [N5-F3]. This means that computational models must account for boundary conditions such as fluid flow direction, shear rate, and flow-induced rheotaxis, as well as flow regimes that can either guide sperm or eliminate poorly motile sperm [N2-F2][N5-F3].

### 4. Experimental methods for characterizing tubal-fluid properties

The branch report on experimental methods shows that pH, osmolarity, and viscosity can be measured with standard and specialized techniques. For pH and osmolarity, the evidence indicates that these properties can be measured in raw semen or seminal plasma, and that the processes involved in measurement are discussed in the literature [N5-R5]. For viscosity, the evidence points to microfluidic and rheological methods, including microfluidic rheology, rotational rheometers, automated capillary viscometers, and microfluidic-based VROC methods [N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R4]. These methods are important because they allow accurate quantification of fluid rheology, which is critical for modeling sperm movement [N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R4].

Experimental conditions affect reproducibility. The evidence shows that sample handling and loading procedures matter, as indicated by the video on loading low-viscosity samples on a rotational rheometer [N6-R5]. It also notes that microfluidic rheology is time- and sample-efficient, suggesting that measurement speed and precision can improve reproducibility [N6-R2]. However, the evidence does not explicitly state how much variability remains across methods, so any claim about reproducibility must be cautious. The broader implication is that reproducibility depends on standardizing both the measurement method and the sample conditions, such as temperature, shear history, and sample handling [N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R5].

There are also limitations in translating lab measurements to in vivo tubal fluid. The evidence indicates that tubal-fluid rheology is complex and species-dependent, with viscosity varying along the reproductive tract, during the menstrual cycle, and between species [N5-F3]. This variation means that laboratory measurements may not capture the full in vivo complexity of tubal fluid. The same study also notes that conventional microscopy and population-level studies have restricted understanding of how flow and viscosity combine at the single-cell level [N5-F3]. This suggests that lab measurements may miss the dynamic, single-cell interactions and fluid-flow effects that occur in the tubal environment. The evidence on epithelial-cell response to elevated viscosity in culture media further implies that fluid properties can induce changes in tissue function, which may not be fully reproduced in simple in vitro measurements [N6-R3].

### 5. Modeling implications of tubal-fluid physics

The modeling implications are clear. Inaccurate fluid assumptions can bias model predictions because the physical properties of tubal fluid are not neutral background conditions but active determinants of sperm behavior. The upstream evidence shows that viscosity, osmolarity, and pH directly influence sperm motility, trajectory, and energetics, with viscosity having a dominant effect on flagellar waveform and higher viscosities associated with increased flagellar amplitude [N2-F2][N5-F3]. It also reports that pH affects motility, with reduced pH decreasing sperm motility linearly [N5-R2]. These findings mean that if a model assumes a uniform, static fluid environment or ignores flow and shear effects, it may misrepresent how sperm swim, turn, and respond to tubal-fluid conditions [N5-F3].

Which simplifications are acceptable versus which are limiting depends on the modeling goal and the level of detail required. The evidence supports some simplifications, but also warns against over-simplification. For example, the review on sperm swimming notes that computational studies can use both simplified theoretical methods and more detailed numerical approaches [N3-R3]. This implies that simplified models can be useful for capturing general patterns or testing hypotheses, while more detailed models are better for capturing the complex interactions between flagellar mechanics, fluid dynamics, and environmental conditions [N3-R3]. However, the evidence also indicates that some properties are more important than others. The experimental study on flagellar energetics shows that viscosity is more dominant than shear rate in shaping flagellar waveform and that the synergistic effect of flow and viscosity is important for energy-efficient beating behavior [N5-F3]. This means that models can safely simplify shear rate where viscosity is the main driver, but they should not eliminate viscosity altogether. Likewise, the upstream evidence on tubal-fluid properties suggests that pH and osmolarity should be included as measurable variables because they influence motility and survival [N2-F2][N5-R2]. In contrast, assumptions that ignore flow-induced rheotaxis, boundary conditions, or the dynamic interplay between viscosity and sperm flagellar mechanics are likely to be limiting [N2-F2][N5-F3].

Fluid dynamics affect sperm navigation, collision, and fertilization likelihood in three major ways. First, flow and viscosity can guide sperm navigation. The experimental study reports that flow-induced rheotaxis selects sperm capable of swimming against the flow toward the egg, while higher shear rates and flow can change flagellar curvature, peak energy, and lateral head displacement [N5-F3]. This means that models that do not account for flow will fail to capture how sperm orient and move toward the egg. Second, fluid dynamics influence collision likelihood. The same study notes that in a viscoelastic environment, both the linearity of the swimming trajectory and the curvature at the flagellar tip are amplified by viscosity, which can increase progressive thrust and make hyperactivated sperm more effective at penetrating mucus and oviduct fluid [N5-F3]. This implies that viscosity can change how sperm interact with each other and with the surrounding fluid, altering the probability of collisions. Third, fluid dynamics affect fertilization likelihood by selecting sperm based on motility and quality. The review on reproductive tract microenvironment states that fluid flow and other cues filter low-quality sperm and select high-quality sperm for fertilization [N2-F2]. The experimental evidence also indicates that non-sufficiently motile sperm are more likely to be extruded from the competition, while highly motile sperm can swim against the flow and improve DNA integrity [N5-F3]. So, fluid dynamics do not merely passively transport sperm; they actively shape which sperm reach the egg and which are eliminated [N2-F2][N5-F3].

### 6. Bottom line

In short, tubal-fluid physics matters for modeling fertilization and sperm movement because tubal fluid is the biologically relevant environment where sperm and egg meet, where capacitation and fertilization occur, and where sperm must navigate, survive, and compete. Its measurable properties—viscosity, osmolarity, and pH—directly influence sperm motility, trajectory, and energetics [N2-F2][N5-F3][N5-R2]. Experimental methods exist to characterize these properties, but they are not perfect and may not fully capture in vivo complexity [N5-F3][N6-R3]. Modeling implications are therefore clear: inaccurate fluid assumptions can bias predictions, some simplifications are acceptable, and fluid dynamics profoundly affect sperm navigation, collision, and fertilization likelihood [N2-F2][N5-F3][N3-R3].
